stem: A client with vomiting and poor intake is clinically volume depleted and has an elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN). Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The elevation can support a prerenal process from water depletion or reduced renal perfusion when interpreted with the clinical picture and other renal data.
options.B: The elevation specifically establishes postrenal urinary obstruction, making the client's volume depletion clinically unrelated to the laboratory result.
options.C: The elevation indicates improved renal clearance because BUN rises as glomerular filtration becomes more efficient during volume depletion.
options.D: The elevation should be treated as unrelated to hydration or perfusion, so it does not contribute to assessment of this volume-depleted client.

rationale: Current Mayo Clinic Laboratories information lists water depletion from decreased intake or excessive loss and cardiac decompensation/reduced perfusion among prerenal causes of increased BUN. Mayo also lists renal and postrenal causes and notes that BUN is often interpreted with serum creatinine to help distinguish prerenal, renal, and postrenal hyperuremia. In this client with vomiting, poor intake, and clinical volume depletion, A is the appropriate interpretation. B overstates specificity for obstruction, C reverses the relationship to renal clearance, and D incorrectly dismisses the relevance of hydration and perfusion.
educational_objective: Interpret elevated BUN as a nonspecific finding that can support prerenal azotemia in a volume-depleted client when integrated with clinical status and other renal data.
source_version_date: Current Test Catalog; generated test definition May 13, 2026; live page rechecked 2026-08-26
source_locator: Clinical Information: increased BUN may result from prerenal causes including cardiac decompensation and water depletion from decreased intake/excessive loss; renal and postrenal causes also listed; BUN is frequently requested with serum creatinine to aid differential diagnosis.
source_claim_supported: Elevated BUN in a volume-depleted client can support a prerenal process from water depletion or reduced perfusion but is not etiologically specific by itself.
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpret laboratory findings and trends and integrate diagnostic data with client condition.
correction_summary: Balanced option lengths and preserved BUN as contextual evidence rather than a stand-alone etiologic diagnosis.

audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — Mayo explicitly lists both prerenal water depletion and nonprerenal causes, so A is the only appropriately qualified interpretation.
